overview: Albertosaurus sarcophagus was a large albertosaurine tyrannosaur from the latest Campanian of Alberta (~70 Ma), slightly younger than Gorgosaurus and preceding the arrival of Tyrannosaurus. A single remarkable bonebed in the Horseshoe Canyon Formation preserves at least 26 Albertosaurus individuals of varying ages — the strongest direct fossil evidence for gregarious behaviour in any tyrannosaur.

The Horseshoe Canyon bonebed, discovered by Barnum Brown in 1910 and re-excavated by Philip Currie from 1997, shows a bimodal size distribution: a few large adults and many sub-adults and juveniles. This pattern is consistent with group hunting or at least seasonal aggregation, though the exact nature of the grouping remains debated.

articles.title: Discovery and the Dry Island bonebed
articles.body: Albertosaurus was named by Osborn in 1905 from Barnum Brown's material collected along the Red Deer River. Brown himself found the bonebed in 1910 but collected only a few specimens before moving on. Philip Currie re-excavated it from 1997 onward, revealing the full scale of the multi-individual accumulation. The flood hypothesis — multiple animals killed by a catastrophic flood — competes with the pack-hunting interpretation.

articles.title: Anatomy
articles.body: Albertosaurus had a relatively gracile build compared to Tyrannosaurus, with proportionally longer legs adapted for sustained pursuit. The skull deepened significantly with age, and the adult dentition was well suited to bone crushing. Like all tyrannosaurids, it had vestigial two-fingered forelimbs.

articles.title: Ecological role
articles.body: In the Horseshoe Canyon ecosystem Albertosaurus was the sole large tyrannosaur, preying on hadrosaurs (Edmontosaurus, Hypacrosaurus) and smaller ornithischians. The bimodal bonebed age distribution — adults rare, juveniles common — matches predictions from models of gregarious pack-hunting where younger animals performed the pursuit while large adults delivered the killing bite.

fossilRecord.material: Many specimens including skulls, skeletons and a multispecimen bonebed preserving an estimated 12–26 individuals.
fossilRecord.paleo: Late Cretaceous coastal plain environments of western Canada.
fossilRecord.evidence: The Dry Island bonebed provides the best evidence for social or group behaviour in any large theropod.

record.description: Albertosaurus sarcophagus was an albertosaurine tyrannosaurid from the lower Horseshoe Canyon Formation of Alberta. Numerous skulls and skeletons spanning growth stages, including a multi-individual bonebed, make it one of the better represented large theropods.
facts: The Dry Island bonebed preserves many individuals but does not by itself prove coordinated pack hunting.
Its lighter build and long hind limbs relative to Tyrannosaurus are anatomically supported; precise speed is not.

presentation.heroLead: A lightly built tyrannosaurid from Late Cretaceous Alberta, known from many skulls and skeletons and from a bonebed that preserves animals of different ages together.

animalParagraphs: Albertosaurus was a large two-legged predator of the tyrannosaur family, smaller and more slender than Tyrannosaurus, with a long, low skull, a deep lower jaw and small bony hornlets above the eyes. Adults are estimated at roughly eight to nine metres long, with body mass estimates of around two tonnes depending on the method used.

The skull carried a single row of thick, serrated teeth in each jaw and was built to withstand heavy loading, which supports a bite-driven feeding style. The two-fingered arms were very short. Bone histology shows that individuals grew fastest in their teenage years and reached full size at around twenty, with the oldest known animal about twenty-eight years old.

Its long shins and feet relative to its thigh are anatomically real, and are usually read as signs of a relatively agile animal for its size. What Albertosaurus actually ate, how fast it moved and whether the animals in the Dry Island bonebed lived together are interpretations rather than direct observations.
animalHighlights: A long, low skull with prominent hornlets above the eyes distinguishes albertosaurines from the deeper-skulled tyrannosaurines.
Proportionally long hindlimbs and a lighter build than Tyrannosaurus are directly visible in the skeletons.
A growth series from juveniles to old adults is one of the best for any large theropod.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.level: Supported by teeth and jaw anatomy
lifeCards.reason: Robust serrated teeth and a strongly built skull indicate a predatory or scavenging carnivore. No gut contents are known, so specific prey is inferred from the fauna it lived alongside.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: The hindlimb proportions are longer than in Tyrannosaurus of the same body size, but absolute running speed cannot be measured from bones alone.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: Length is well constrained by several large individuals; mass estimates of roughly 1.7–2.5 tonnes depend on the modelling method.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: Overall proportions come from articulated skeletons. No skin impressions are confirmed for Albertosaurus itself, so scales, any feathering and colour are inferred from relatives.

whereFacts.label: Type locality
whereFacts.value: Red Deer River valley near Kneehills Creek, Alberta, Canada

locality.name: Red Deer River valley
locality.note: Horseshoe Canyon Formation. The holotype was collected in 1884 by Joseph Tyrrell; the Dry Island bonebed lies further downstream in the same formation.

presentation.classificationSummary: Albertosaurus is a tyrannosaurid and the name-bearing genus of Albertosaurinae, the more slender branch of the family that also contains Gorgosaurus. The two genera are so similar that some workers have united them, but most current analyses keep them separate.

related.reason: Its closest relative, an older albertosaurine from the Dinosaur Park Formation that some authors have merged with Albertosaurus.
A contemporary-region tyrannosaurine with a deeper, heavier skull for comparison with the albertosaurine build.
The larger, more robust tyrannosaurine that replaced albertosaurines at the very end of the Cretaceous.

questions.title: Did Albertosaurus hunt in groups?
questions.copy: The Dry Island bonebed holds at least a dozen individuals of different ages. Whether they died together as a social group or were gathered by a flood or other event is still debated; the bonebed alone does not prove pack behaviour.

questions.title: Is Gorgosaurus the same genus?
questions.copy: Gorgosaurus libratus has at times been placed in Albertosaurus. Detailed cranial comparisons support keeping them apart, but the question turns on how much difference a genus should contain.

questions.title: How fast could it run?
questions.copy: Its long legs suggest a relatively quick animal for a large theropod, but speed estimates rely on biomechanical models and vary widely.

review.ageReviewNote: Well-supported A. sarcophagus occurrences are early Maastrichtian in the lower Horseshoe Canyon Formation.

specimens.name: Holotype
specimens.note: Partial skull collected by Joseph Tyrrell in 1884; the basis of Osborn's 1905 name. CMN 5600, another partial skull, is the paratype.

specimens.name: Dry Island bonebed
specimens.note: Bones of at least a dozen individuals of different growth stages from one site in Dry Island Buffalo Jump Provincial Park.

panel.headline: Dozens of individuals, from a partial holotype skull to a multi-animal bonebed.
panel.standfirst: Albertosaurus sarcophagus is known from many skulls and partial to near-complete skeletons in the Horseshoe Canyon Formation of Alberta, including a single bonebed that preserves juveniles, subadults and adults together. The name rests on a partial skull collected in 1884.

coverage.label: Excellent
coverage.basis: Every region of the skeleton is represented by multiple individuals across a growth series, and several skeletons are substantially complete, although no single skeleton is entirely so.

metrics.label: Key limitation
metrics.value: No confirmed skin or soft tissue

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: Complete and partial skulls with dentition, cervical, dorsal, sacral and caudal vertebrae, ribs and gastralia, pectoral and pelvic girdles, forelimbs, hindlimbs and feet, from individuals ranging from small juveniles to old adults.
knownRemains.note: Some historical specimens were once referred to other tyrannosaurids, and the type series itself was re-examined in 2010, so referral of older material should be checked against the modern revisions.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: Many complete and partial skulls with teeth, including the holotype and paratype partial skulls in Ottawa and well-preserved skulls in Drumheller.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Cervical, dorsal, sacral and caudal series, ribs, gastralia and chevrons in several articulated skeletons.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Shoulder and hip girdles, two-fingered forelimbs, and hindlimbs and feet across the growth series.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: Bone histology preserved and sampled for growth studies; healed injuries and jaw lesions recorded. No confirmed skin impressions, feathers, colour or gut contents.

specimenCards.title: CMN 5601 · holotype
specimenCards.description: A partial skull collected by Joseph Tyrrell in 1884 from the Red Deer River valley. It passed through the names Laelaps and Dryptosaurus incrassatus before Henry Fairfield Osborn made it the type of Albertosaurus sarcophagus in 1905. A second partial skull, CMN 5600, is the paratype.
specimenCards.meta: Red Deer River near Kneehills Creek · Horseshoe Canyon Formation · Canadian Museum of Nature

specimenCards.title: Dry Island bonebed · TMP 1998.063 series
specimenCards.description: Found by Barnum Brown in 1910 and relocated by Philip Currie in 1997, the site has yielded bones from at least a dozen and possibly more than twenty individuals of different ages, all attributed to A. sarcophagus.
specimenCards.meta: Dry Island Buffalo Jump Provincial Park · Horseshoe Canyon Formation · Royal Tyrrell Museum

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: Many skulls and skeletons spanning juvenile to adult stages, growth rings in sampled bones, and a mass-death assemblage of one species.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: A relatively lightly built tyrannosaurid predator that grew rapidly in its teens; the bonebed is interpreted by some as evidence of gregarious behaviour.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: Whether the bonebed animals lived as a group, the animal's external covering and colour, its speed, and precise adult body mass.
